paragraphs.text: “The actual significance of the word sáhitya [loosely, "literature"] is inherent in the word itself. Sáhitya is defined as 'that whose characteristic is to move with (sahita = ‘with’) the trends of lifeʼ… The word sáhitya can be interpreted in another way as well: sa + hita = hitena saha, 'that which co-exists with hita [welfare]ʼ. Where there is no inner spirit of welfare, we cannot use the term sáhitya. The creations or compositions of those who proclaim, ‘Art for artʼs sake,ʼ cannot be treated as sáhitya… Thus literature is that which moves together with society and leads society towards true fulfilment and welfare by providing the inspiration to serve. The statement ‘Art for artʼs sakeʼ is not acceptable; rather we should say, 'Art for service and blessedness.ʼ… Those who are inferior and neglected, helpless and destitute – whom society considers to be infernal maggots – are the very people who are the most unrepresented in the salons of literature… The sáhityika or the artist has to take the responsibility of enabling them to rise up and sit in the same row with the rest of society, after dusting off the dirt from their bodies…

paragraphs.text: Shrii Prabhat Ranjan Sarkar (also known as Shrii Shrii Ánandamúrti, a spiritual Guru) elaborately explained his views on art and literature in the discourse (“Art and Literature”, A Few Problems Solved Part 1) quoted above. But he did not stop there. Going a step further, he translated his words into actions, giving a direct example by creating his own literature, which is marked by his natural ease and aptitude. Thus a great series named Sarkarʼs Short Stories was written in fourteen parts. In June 1985, the first Bengali fourteen-part series was published under the authorʼs direct guidance. In January 1990, the English Sarkarʼs Short Stories Part 1 was published. Since then, there has been a persistent demand from our esteemed readers for the publication of all the parts. In response to that, in October 2010, a volume named Sarkarʼs Short Stories Parts 1-3 in one volume was published. Now, we are extremely happy to publish Sarkarʼs Short Stories Parts 4, 5, 6. Genuine and sincere efforts are going on to publish all the remaining parts within the next year. We fervently hope to fulfil this objective with the cooperation of all concerned.

paragraphs.text: All stories belonging to the Sarkarʼs Short Stories series appeared originally as important and integral parts of the authorʼs writings on a vast range of topics from linguistics and philology to history, geography, medicine, science, art, religion, spirituality, philosophy, etc. Such books included Varńa Vijiṋána, Varńa Vicitrá (eight parts) and Shabda Cayaniká (twenty-six parts). Like most great authors, Shrii Prabhat Ranjan Sarkar is a consummate storyteller, thus he used in those books a seemingly inexhaustible supply of anecdotes, personal experiences and interesting as well as educative references, in order to capture the readerʼs interest. And it is mostly those stories that have been excerpted to constitute the present book. Thus it is natural that in the stories contained in the present book, we will find, either at the beginnings of those stories or as footnotes, relevant references to the linguistic and other subjects of the original books. In this way the stories retain the authenticity of the original books.

paragraphs.text: The verbal root bat́ means to grow, to acquire strength, to exhibit strength. In common parlance, the ba that we get by adding d́a to the verbal root bat́ means “one that gathers strength or displays strength”. The banyan tree does not stop growing. So one meaning of ba (bat́ + d́a) is banyan tree. Bat́ > bad́a > baŕa.

paragraphs.text: In Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh, a banyan tree is colloquially referred to as bar. In Persian and Urdu it is called bargad. The banyan tree belongs to the family of trees which does not stop growing; it keeps on growing. There are many species ( 1 ) of banyan tree in the world; among them, the Chinese and Indian species are the most noteworthy. The Indian banyan tree (Banian indica) grows aerial roots ( 2 ) from its main trunk rather quickly. These aerial roots later grow into trunks. Some banyan trees have a large number of trunks. Sometimes it happens that even after the original trunk has been eaten up by white ants ( 3 ) [termites] or caterpillars, the tree survives and remains in good health due to its well-developed aerial roots. The banyan tree in the botanical garden of Kolkata and the banyan tree standing in the vicinity of Bagchi-Jamshedpur in Nadia District are estimated to be more than four thousand years old. In fact, the second one may be even older. Many people say that the banyan tree obtained its unending longevity as a boon from Sita. Let me briefly tell you that [mythological] story.

This aerial root (bat́er jhuri) is very good for dysentery. If an aerial root is cut into pieces, mixed with rice water (water in which rice has been washed) and then taken on an empty stomach, it serves as an effective antidote to dysentery.

The name Gaya comes from Gaya Káshyapa, the name of an eminent scholar in Magadha at that time. During that period, Gaya Káshyapa, Nadii Káshyapa and Urubilva Káshyapa were the three great scholars living in Magadha. It was after Urubilva Káshyapa that a village on the bank of the river Nairanjana where Buddha received enlightenment was named. It was also here that Buddhaʼs cousin, Sujátá, queen of the local feudal potentate, saved the life of Buddha by feeding him sweet rice porridge. The actual name of the village Arval in the present Gaya District is Urubilva.
Shopping means buying (pańan) and marketing means selling (vipańan). Some people use the word marketing for buying. No, it is not marketing, [that is actually shopping].

paragraphs.text: The son of King Balii was King Báńa. King Báńa was a devotee of Lord Shiva. Báńeshvar, one of the names of Lord Shiva, is derived from the name of King Báńa. The historical King Báńa was possibly a king of some part of Bengal. There are certain places in Bengal which are named after him; for example, Báńaeshvar and Báńagaŕ. In common parlance, one of the meanings of the word ba that we get by adding the suffix d́a to the verbal root bal is Balii, the demon King. It is this King Balii who is better known as MahaBalii. King Balii, who is still highly regarded in the most remote parts of Kerala in South India, is invariably associated with the name of Viśńu or Náráyańa. Náráyańa defeated King Balii not by physical strength but by the strength of intellect. The word ba that we get by adding the suffix d́a to the verbal root bal means that intellectual strength is the greatest strength, and it refers to Viśńu. ( 2 )

paragraphs.text: The word ba does not only mean one who is physically strong; it is equally applicable to one who is mentally or spiritually strong. That is why the word ba, which is used to mean the application of physical force, is also used to mean the application of mental or spiritual force. So, one of the meanings of ba, which we get by adding the suffix d́a to the verbal root bal is to create pressure, to create circumstantial pressure or to proceed according to a plan in order to attain some particular goal. Some people think that the word ba means to vilify someone. This is partly true. One can use the word ba when someone is vilified in order to pressurise that person into doing something. So the verbal root ba + d́a = ba means “to pressurise in order to attain a particular goal”.

paragraphs.text: Pat́olprasanna was a simple man who minded his own business, but his pious wife Smt. Begunbálá – well, who could withstand her speech! The torrential flow of words from her mouth was stronger than that of a western gale. Every day, she would religiously quarrel with Pat́olprasanna every fifteen minutes by the clock. She said that in this world, a man should work and one who did not work was sure to be ruined. The best kind of work was quarrelling. The kind of majesty that a serious quarrel invoked has hardly any comparison in the cosmos. When the quarrel reached its climax, Begunbálá would bring out her jewellery box, remove the ornaments from her body and put them in the box. Then she would put a lock on the box and check at least thrice to see that the box had been properly locked. After that, she would tie the key into a knot at the end of her saree and tuck it in her vest. Finally, she would hold the box in her hand and say, “Well, Mister, I am going now. I have decided to drown myself. Let me see which female ghost serves you food!”

Whenever the quarrel became serious, Jhiuṋgeráńii would say, “Má, you saw my father standing on the bank of the pond that day. He admitted that you were a goddess dropped from heaven. You must have seen that all the gods and goddesses have weapons in their hands. One who has two hands has weapons in both hands. One who has four hands has weapons in all four hands. footnotes.text: Pat́ol is a Sanskrit word, which means a particular vegetable [wax gourd or pointed gourd]. One of the meanings of pat́ol is ‘many’; another meaning of pat́ol is eyelid. At the time of death, the eyelid moves slightly upward.Hence, death is often described lightly as pat́ol tolá. The Sanskrit word for paltá [pat́ol leaf] is pat́olpatram. People who do not eat fish publicly but only secretly describe fish as jala pat́ol in Sanskrit.
Pat́ol (pointed gourd), begun (brinjal), jhiṋge (ridge-gourd) and Dhyáṋrash (ladies finger) are names of different vegetables.–Trans.

paragraphs.text: One of the meanings of the word bha that we obtain by adding the suffix d́a to the verbal root bha is “shining opulence”. There may be opulence of prestige, honour, money, quality or wisdom, but when that opulence is associated with welfare, then the word bha is used to indicate this. Please remember that opulence alone cannot elevate opulence to the category of bha. This means that the financial opulence of a rich man does not automatically come under the category of bha. Someoneʼs wealth may be bha while someone elseʼs may not be.

paragraphs.text: During my childhood, I heard that Manindra Chandra Nandi, the great, bountiful king of Kashim Bazar [Murshidabad District], never disappointed anyone. He thought that God had given him wealth to spend for public welfare. A time came when his estate sustained a huge loss on account of his charitable disposition, and the government acquired it under “Court of Words” [a legal term to acquire zaminderʼs property in British period]. In other words, his estate was run by government officers, and the king was given a limited monthly pension to meet the expenses of his family. As a result, the charity of the king was about to end and the poor people felt miserable. They prayed, “Let the wealth of the king grow more and more.” Since the king had spent his wealth on public welfare, this kind of wealth may be considered as bha.

footnotes.text: Shreśt́hii > shet́t́hii > shet́hii > shet́h; in South India, cet́t́i. In ancient India, the owner of 500,000 (five lakhs) gold coins (siinak) was called a Shreśt́hii.
Kalákanda is a type of very high quality sweet made of condensed milk; ghior is a sweet dish prepared in western India with liberal quantities of ghee.
Here in our locality [when the author was residing in Jamalpur], a beyái is called samdhii.

Umdá was originally a Persian word. Some words used in Hindustani, such as umdá, paráyá [owned by others] and buland [height] do not change their gender according to the gender of the noun they qualify. An object of high quality will be called umdá ciij and not umdi ciij, although the word ciij is feminine. Similarly, one has to use paráyá even before a feminine noun and not parayii. It is a common error to write or say paráyii. The word buland will also remain unchanged before a noun whether the noun is masculine or feminine. The word bulandii is an abstract noun; it means “height”.

paragraphs.text: Yes, we were talking about the notorious Cáoyá-Cát́á [the amusing name means “always asking for”] Cát́ujje. He was an eminent person in Chinsura-Carakdaunga. I hope some of you know my acquaintance, Hyáḿlá Hoṋdal Hotá. Some of you must know him. (A farmer by profession, he hailed from Halimpur, Hooghly District, Khatian [ledger] No. 3 Plot No. 300). Hyáḿlá Hoṋdal [Hyáḿlá means “greedy”] was not a bad boy, but he was particularly fond of attending feasts. Quite often, he used to wangle an invitation to a feast by asking for it. Sometimes, he would eat at a feast given on the occasions of various rituals, such as shráddha [obsequies] and paite [the ceremony of putting on the holy thread sacramentally for the first time] without an invitation. He had long hair. While eating, he would bend his head in such a way that his face was screened by his hair. The host, when checking the guests to see who were invited and who were not, could not confirm whether he had actually been invited because his face could not be seen. His younger brother, Barśá Bádal, was not so resourceful. As a result, he was not lucky enough to get invitations to feasts.

paragraphs.text: He said, “I asked Cáoyá-Cát́á, 'Am I really invited today?ʼ Cáoyá-Cát́á at once replied, 'Certainly, of course. Not once, but hundred times, yes.ʼ After a brief pause, Cáoyá-Cát́á told me, 'Man has progressed a lot in observing formalities. Whatever it is, whether one sincerely likes formality or not, it is written on the wedding invitation card, ‘Blessing in place of formality is desirable’. But actually, everybody wants formality instead of blessing. You will notice that there is a practice of keeping a written record of who has presented what to the bride and the bridegroom in wedding homes. Obviously, such an account is maintained because there is a hankering, in the deepest recesses of the mind for these presents. Not only that, you will see that if somebodyʼs marriage takes place towards the end of the month, the ceremony of bau-bhát [the ceremony of a bride serving food for the first time to her husbandʼs kinsfolk] is not held then because by the end of the month, everybodyʼs pocket is empty. The guests may not come at all because they are unable to give presents. And those who do come would not be able to give costly presents. Keeping this in view, bau-bhát is arranged at the beginning of the next month a few days after the marriage. At that time, the guests are quite solvent. Moreover, not much money is spent on feeding because it is written on the invitation card that the entertainment of the guests will be in keeping with the rules of ‘guest control’. It means that just by giving a light refreshment, it is possible to squeeze an expensive gift.

paragraphs.text: In the consonantal scheme of alphabets, the first letter in the ka group is ka and the last letter in the pa group is ma. Now the question is: why does ka come first and ma last? This world revolves around the process of creation, preservation and destruction. The seed of creation is a; that is why a comes first in the vowels. First creation, and only then do the rest follow. After that is u, the seed of preservation. So creation is spread over these three sounds. The combination of these three sounds is called ońḿ (a + u + m = ońḿ).
summary: In the consonantal scheme of alphabets, the first letter in the ka group is ka and the last letter in the pa group is ma. Now the question is: why does ka come

paragraphs.text: Ka is the seed of action of Brahma. In other words, one part of the Supreme Brahma continues to exist as the cause while the other part is manifested in action. One part is the cause and the other part is the effect or objectivated cause. That is why this ka is called saḿvrttibodhicitta in Buddhist philosophy. Since ka is the seed of action, ka is therefore the first consonant; and since ma is the seed of destruction, ma is the last consonant.
summary: Ka is the seed of action of Brahma. In other words, one part of the Supreme Brahma continues to exist as the cause while the other part is manifested in action.

paragraphs.text: I was talking about ouṋḿkára – a + u + m = ońḿ. But this om is meant for the manifested world. If one wants to use the seed of some positive sound for both the manifested and the unmanifested, then om will not do; one has to write oṋḿ [like Bengali symbol]. In this case, the candrabindu [the diacritical mark of a point in the crescent moon indicating a nasalised sound] connotes Nirguńa Brahma [Brahma without attributes]. This Brahma without attributes cannot be verbalised in utterance. So, in orthography, one first uses a point (a point has a position but no magnitude) and the longish sign that looks like a crescent moon under the point indicates the transformation from the negative to the positive aspect of attributes. In Sanskrit, it is called náda, that is, nirguńa saḿsthiti [the state of non-attributes] is transformed into Saguńa Brahma [the state of attributes] with the help of náda or sound. Please remember that it is not exactly a candrabindu [a point with a curve suggestive of the crescent moon]. It is something like the Bengali iishvara sign (a symbol put before the name of a deceased person). According to old custom, this nádabinducihna is used before the name of a dead person. When reading this nádabindu, we read it as iishvara. When a man is alive, the word shrii is used before his name; for example, Shrii Kumud Chandra Maiti. But the prefix Shrii cannot be used before his name after his death. The name Kumud Chandra Maiti will be written just after nadabindu and the name will be read as iishvara Kumud Chandra Maiti.

paragraphs.text: Another name of oṋḿkára is prańava, the etymological meaning of which is “that which propels towards the destination.” You are probably aware of the fact that in ancient times, in that age of superstition, not everyone had the right to articulate the word oṋḿkára. The outcastes and women were not only disallowed from uttering the word oṋḿ, even their right to hear the word was constrained. Hearsay has it that if any of them heard the oṋḿkára sound, molten lead would be poured into their ears to make them completely deaf. Verily, what an age of superstition it was! Such superstitions pervaded all walks of life. It was not only women who were tortured on account of this; men suffered no less. A story of social superstition comes to mind. The story is about one Subuddhi Roy of the Pathan dynasty.

paragraphs.text: Subuddhi Roy was the Prime Minister of Bengal during the reign of the Pathans. In addition to his political stature, he enjoyed great social prestige as well. On one particular occasion, some water from a Muslimʼs badná [a small pitcher with a slender spout] accidentally touched his face. The Brahman pundits convened a meeting. They unanimously resolved that it was a serious sin, a serious crime. Subuddhi Roy would have to perform a ceremonial expiation. Oh, I forgot to tell you that Subuddhi Roy at that time was the head of the Brahman community, a representative of the Brahmans.

paragraphs.text: As the Brahman community rose in arms against Subuddhi Roy, he became frightened to the extreme. He was made to seek the counsel of the pundits of Nabadwip [Navadviip] for the necessary mode of expiation. The pundits of Nabadwip gave the verdict that he had to perform tuśáńal práyashcitta [expiation with fire made from husks or chaff]. In tuśáńal práyashcitta, the guilty person had to stand before the fire when it was fully ablaze. The husks would be spread over an area covering sixty-four times the height of the person. The sinner or guilty person had to walk barefoot on it. If the sinner survived the ordeal, the expiation would be accomplished. And if the sinner died, the matter ended there.

paragraphs.text: One meaning of the Sanskrit verbal root mada is “what gives pleasure in sucking”. Etymologically, it means water, cordial, sharbat [sweet drink], hyacinth, fruit juice and any kind of fluid which comes under the category of drinks. The kind of thirst that one feels after consuming the items mentioned above is called mada + d́a = ma. For example, one feels thirsty when one takes chátu [flour made of barley, pigeon-pea, maize, etc.] in a small quantity of water. Again, one feels thirsty when taking poláo [a highly spiced dish of rice and meat boiled in clarified butter]. This kind of thirst for water is called jaltán.

paragraphs.text: Food (in the sense of the verbal root ma) which does not cause any trouble upon its ingestion is called ma. This kind of food does not require much chewing and usually goes down the throat almost as soon as it has been put into the mouth; for example, birikaláyer dál [blackgram pulse], kuler ambal, pát́ or pát-shák [green leaves of jute plant] with a touch of salt and pepper and items prepared with basella are quite wholesome and can easily be eaten. That is why, by adding the suffix d́a to the verbal root mada or by adding the suffix ka to the verbal root má, we get the word ma to mean this kind of food.

paragraphs.text: There lived a Brahman and his wife. The Brahman was a very good man, as simple and ever cheerful as Lord Shiva. His wife was also a very good person, but she was rather fond of eating – in particular, the attraction of basella was irresistible to her. Ut́hone yedike cái keval puiṋ dekhite pái [in whichever direction of the courtyard I look, only basella comes to view]. The Brahman also ate basella but did not like it much. After eating some pántá bhát [stale rice] and hot beguni [a fried snack prepared by dipping slices of brinjal in a thin paste of pulse powder] with a sprinkle of salt and pepper, he would leave the house for various kinds of work. His wife took care of the household chores. After some time, it was noticed that the Brahman was getting more and more emaciated while his wife was getting heavier by the day. The people of the locality enquired, “Oh Brahman, what has happened to you? You are getting thinner and thinner and your wife is becoming heavier and heavier! What is the mystery? Certainly, after treating you with a pot of stale rice and packing you off, your wife must be preparing seven hundred kinds of delicious food and eating them with relish afterwards.”

paragraphs.text: In ancient times, people used the wood of the sal tree (indrakáśt́ha), marmelos tree (bel kát́h) and fig tree (ud́umbar) as firewood in religious sacrifices. There are several species of ud́umbar or d́umur [fig] of which the common fig and sacrificial fig [Ficus religiosa] are important. It is this sacrificial fig which is called ud́umbar or yájiṋad́umbar. Both these kinds of figs are good for the liver and kidney. They are also medicines for blood pressure. Sacrificial fig is more nutritious and more easily digestible than the common fig.
summary: In ancient times, people used the wood of the sal tree (indrakáśt́ha), marmelos tree (bel kát́h) and fig tree (ud́umbar) as firewood in religious sacrifices.

Since it blossoms inside, we call it a fruit, and because we cannot see it bloom, we think that a fig flower is a rare thing which cannot be seen. When someone makes an appearance after a long time, we usually say to that person, “Whatʼs the matter? We donʼt see you at all these days! We wonder if you have turned into a fig flower!” A fig is called d́umar in the Angika language while in most parts of North India it is called gullar.

The whole world looked up to Magadha for wisdom and spiritual wealth (upasampadá). There were many famous Buddhist monasteries in the land of Magadha. In the beginning, these were called Brahmavihár. Later, they came to be known as Baoddhavihár or Buddhist monasteries. Phullarháriibihár was one of the monasteries in Magadha. Phullarháriibihár was later renamed Phulawariishariif. In those days, milk and curd of excellent quality were available in Phullarháriibihár. Cowherds and curd sellers were also to be found in abundance. They were truly skilled in their craft.

When he reached there, the tired curd seller sat under a tree to rest. He sat under the tree for quite some time. While resting, he became drowsy. By the way, I forgot to tell you that he did not have weighing instruments – on one side of the pole that he was carrying on his shoulders was a mund of curd and on the other side was a stone with a weight (ojan ( 3 )) of one mund.

At first, even after he reached Ajimabad ( 4 ), he did not realise the significance of the four pieces.

The name of the city of Azimabad owed its origin to the name of Azim-ush-san, the commander of the army. Akbar made Azimabad the capital of Bihar when he turned Behar into a subá [province]. During British rule, Azimabad was renamed Patna city. Recently, the name of the city has been changed to Patna Sahib. The Patna city (its real name is Bankipur) we know now did not exist in those days. Kusumpur was at that time situated much farther west near Maner. During Buddhaʼs time, Kusumpur was not the capital of Magadha; the capital was Rajgir (many people call it Rájgrha by mistake; that is not correct. Had it been Rájgrha in the Magahii language, its name would have been Rájghar).

paragraphs.text: With the pursuit of knowledge and subsequent acquisition of scholarship, human beings learn to exercise control over the mind. They train birds and animals to do various things. A restrained mind is the essence of all kinds of knowledge and learning. Otherwise, one can never learn anything nor can one acquire any knowledge and, even if one acquires knowledge, one cannot retain it. The word ya (by adding the suffix d́a to the verbal root yaj) is used for the type of effort by which a human acquires knowledge. It should be borne in mind that, generally, the word ya cannot be used for learning. Only the learning which one tries to acquire for oneʼs own development is called ya. Speaking about development through learning, I am reminded of a story.

paragraphs.text: You must have heard about a place called Singur. In very ancient times, Siḿhapur or Siuṋgur was the capital of Ráŕh. Although Singur was not as old as Bardhaman [Burdwan], it was older than most places in Bengal and India. Later, Singur was completely destroyed by the disastrous flooding of the Damodar River. Anyway, there were two rivers – Pulakitá and Ghrtáci – flowing by Siḿhapur. These rivers were the connecting links between Bhagiirathii and Damodar. Close to Siḿhapur, which was situated on the banks of the confluence of these two rivers, was a now-forgotten port called Siḿhalapát́an. It is said that from the port of Siḿhalpát́an, Vijay Singha, the prince of Ráŕh, set off for Siḿhal [Ceylon], and on reaching Siḿhal conquered the country. This is possibly the reason why the port was named Siḿhalpát́an.

paragraphs.text: In the course of time, the history of the ancient land of Ráŕh was forgotten, and the people of Ráŕh have also forgotten Siḿhalpát́an. At one time, Siḿhapur was not only the seat of royal power but also a centre of learning. In Siḿhapur and the surrounding vicinity there lived many great scholars. Today, that Singur is extinct.

paragraphs.text: You must have heard of the place called Nasipur. Nasipur existed even during the period of the Pathans. During that age, there lived a rajakinii [washerwoman)] who possessed crores of rupees. She would lie down on gold coins. But she would never spend any money, not even a cowry, let alone a copper coin. She said that to spend one cowry meant to lose one rib. For a long time, the washerwoman had been cooking rice in a leaking pot and had been using a broken hand fan to fan herself. This was how she was happily spending her days. But fate was against her. One day, after washing some rice grains and while pouring them into the pitcher, the pitcher cracked from top to bottom from the impact of the rice. The washerwoman felt sad – not because of the cracked pitcher but because so many rice grains that had spilled on the stove were wasted. More saddening was the fact that the fire on the stove was extinguished by the rice and some rice water had spilled on it. With a very heavy heart, she went to Singur. When she reached there, after much bargaining she purchased a pitcher, a hand fan and a small pot of curd because her granddaughter had been pestering her for curd for quite some time.

footnotes.text: In Bengal in those days, human trade [buying and selling of humans] was prevalent. It continued to be prevalent, though on a small scale, toward the end of the Moghul period. There are records of such incidents in the early period of British rule as well. Possibly the last human transaction took place in the district of Bakharganj (Barisal). Portuguese pirates (generally known as hármáds) used to bring boys and girls from East Bengal and the Arakans and sell them in West Bengal. In those days, the dowry system was widespread in Bengal. The author knows that many poor Brahmans could not marry in the district of Burdwan as they were unable to pay the dowry. Hence, some of them would buy girls from these pirates. Nobody bothered about the caste or clan of those girls. In common parlance, they were referred to as bháŕár meye [girls for a price].

paragraphs.text: When we burn an object, the exterior is destroyed by fire, but the interior becomes soft with the heat of the fire. When we ignite an object, both the interior and exterior are destroyed by contact with the fire and are turned into ashes. We burn a brinjal. We ignite the wick of a lamp. When the exterior of an object becomes more or less burnt while the interior does not become very soft but is only slightly affected, we call it singeing. For singeing (jhalsáno), the word ra is applied by adding the suffix d́a to the verbal root rá.

paragraphs.text: In the old days, plays were often very melodramatic. The dialogue of a drama should be natural but it is slightly different from the normal conversations of mundane everyday life. In daily life, when we talk among ourselves, we do not want anyone else to hear us, nor do we think of compelling others to hear us. We confine the conversation to ourselves. But in a dramatic dialogue, the actors have to bear in mind that the audience or spectators should be able to hear what they are saying and should understand from their gestures themselves what they want to say. This is the main difference between normal conversations and dramatic dialogues. Of course, there are other differences as well.

paragraphs.text: The verbal root ruś means not bursting out in anger, to suppress anger. Bursting out in anger is called krodha. But when anger is suppressed, we call it roś. Krodha can be understood immediately, but it takes time to understand roś. Suppose somebody was angry with you and subsequently everything became normal and you have probably forgotten about the incident. Suppose, after quite some time, you invite that person to dinner and he replies harshly, “Iʼm not eating today.” You then realise that he has suppressed anger in his mind. This is called roś.
summary: The verbal root ruś means not bursting out in anger, to suppress anger. Bursting out in anger is called krodha. But when anger is suppressed, we call it roś.

paragraphs.text: Do you know Káliikrpá Bhat́cáj [Kalikripa Bhattacharya] of Shantipur? But how could you know? It happened such a long time ago. It was during the British period. Kálii Bhat́cáj was employed in the civil service in Kashii [Benaras], drawing a fat salary. In those days, anybody who had some knowledge of English could easily get a job. It is said that in those days, the life of a particular class of people consisted of four forms. The first form was for admission to an English medium school. The second form was to obtain a certificate from the school after learning elementary English. The third form was the application form to join the railway service. The fourth form was the platform where one would stand with a railway flag in hand. Kálii Bhat́cháj was much better than these people. And in the meantime, you call me at my home.” Kálii Bhat́cájʼs senior officials who came to visit him were all red-faced Englishmen. So he had no difficulty going on leave because those Englishmen were not familiar with the customs and conventions of this country. Whatever Kálii Bhat́cáj told them, they took it as gospel truth. But life does not always flow smoothly. Finally, an Indian became Kálii Bhat́cájʼs boss. He knew all the local customs. Once, on coming to enquire about Kálii Bhat́cáj, he found him absent from the office. On asking the Establishment Clerk, he came to know that there was no application for leave from Kálii Bhat́cáj. He then issued a ‘show cause chargesheet’ against Kálii Bhat́cáj.

paragraphs.text: In Sanskrit, the verbal root ras means to call by creating a special type of sound; second, to flow; and third, to be sticky. Suppose you are here and on the other side of the vast field stands Khudua Mahato. How would you call him? You will shout, “Oh, Khudua Mahato … ohhhhhhhhh....” To be carried means to flow, to move slightly like a drop of water on a lotus leaf. The third meaning is to feel sticky. For example, glue or mango gum. In all three cases we obtain the word rasa from the verbal root ras. Because of the presence of this juice or rasa, a particular kind of sweet is called rasagollá [round-shaped juicy sweet made of fresh cheese]. There are other such sweets – rasamálái and rasabaŕá.

footnotes.text: The word kalejá was originally Persian. It has become distorted in Bengali.

The Black Hole of Kolkata was a small dungeon in Fort William. It was rumoured that following the fall of the Fort, British and Anglo-Indian soldiers and civilians were held overnight in conditions so cramped that most of them died from suffocation, heat exhaustion and being crushed. The British press carried out a propaganda campaign based on this rumour to justify their occupation of Bengal.

Harekrśńa became impatient. Some wicked people said that one night, he murdered his aunt. There was a police enquiry and lawsuits. footnotes.text: The Sanskrit word for searching for a cow is gaveśańá. Go + eśańáʼ= gaveśańá. In ancient days, hermits and sages living in the forest would send a pupil to search for their cow when it was lost in the forest. They selected a particular pupil who had little interest in studies. He would find the cow after a great deal of hard work and after having spent the entire day looking for it. This kind of extensive search for a cow was called gaveśańá. If a person works very hard to find out the truth about a matter, as hard as the extensive search for a cow, that is also called gaveśańá. In English, the word “research” means gaveśańá.

paragraphs.text: We use the Sanskrit verbal root lup to mean breaking up. When we prepare a programme for a certain event, we divide the time into certain parts or periods. This kind of programme or breaking up of time is also called la. Intelligent human beings apply la to all their work. A good housewife, after lighting the stove, completes the tasks of cleaning the utensils, washing the rooms and other similar work. When the stove is ready, she will first boil the food that takes a long time to cook, then in the meantime she will complete other tasks such as cutting the vegetables, grinding the spices, taking her bath and worshipping. When there is a proper sense of la or organization, human life is fully enriched. Then the work done within oneʼs short, limited life assumes a rich significance, and the drama of life becomes a grand success. Otherwise, even a long life gets lost in darkness from sheer futility. Do you know the story of the weaving couple?

summary: “The actual significance of the word sáhitya [loosely, "literature"] is inherent in the word itself. Sáhitya is defined as 'that whose characteristic is to mo
points.body: “The actual significance of the word sáhitya [loosely, "literature"] is inherent in the word itself. Sáhitya is defined as 'that whose characteristic is to move with (sahita = ‘with’) the trends of lifeʼ… The word sáhitya can be interpreted in another way as well: sa + hita = hitena saha, 'that which co-exists with hita [welfare]ʼ. Where there is no inner spirit of welfare, we cannot use the term sáhitya. The creations or compositions of those who proclaim, ‘Art for artʼs sake,ʼ cannot be treated as sáhitya… Thus literature is that which moves together with society and leads society towards true fulfilment and welfare by providing the inspiration to serve. The statement ‘Art for artʼs sakeʼ is not acceptable; rather we should say, 'Art for service and blessedness.ʼ… Those who are inferior and neglected, helpless and destitute – whom society considers to be infernal maggots – are the very people who are the most unrepresented in the salons of literature… The sáhityika or the artist has to take the responsibility of enabling them to rise up and sit in the same row with the rest of society, after dusting off the dirt from their bodies…

Suspense is equally effective in short stories as in plays; dramatic skill is essential for the writer of those short stories which come in the category of sketches, because a sketch holds an intermediate position between a story and a play. ”

points.body: Shrii Prabhat Ranjan Sarkar (also known as Shrii Shrii Ánandamúrti, a spiritual Guru) elaborately explained his views on art and literature in the discourse (“Art and Literature”, A Few Problems Solved Part 1) quoted above. But he did not stop there. Going a step further, he translated his words into actions, giving a direct example by creating his own literature, which is marked by his natural ease and aptitude. Thus a great series named Sarkarʼs Short Stories was written in fourteen parts. In June 1985, the first Bengali fourteen-part series was published under the authorʼs direct guidance. In January 1990, the English Sarkarʼs Short Stories Part 1 was published. Since then, there has been a persistent demand from our esteemed readers for the publication of all the parts. In response to that, in October 2010, a volume named Sarkarʼs Short Stories Parts 1-3 in one volume was published. Now, we are extremely happy to publish Sarkarʼs Short Stories Parts 4, 5, 6. Genuine and sincere efforts are going on to publish all the remaining parts within the next year. We fervently hope to fulfil this objective with the cooperation of all concerned.

points.title: All stories belonging to the Sarkarʼs Short Stories series appeared originally as importan
points.prompt: Recall and explain from memory: All stories belonging to the Sarkarʼs Short Stories series appeared originally as important and integral parts of the au
summary: All stories belonging to the Sarkarʼs Short Stories series appeared originally as important and integral parts of the authorʼs writings on a vast range of topic
points.body: All stories belonging to the Sarkarʼs Short Stories series appeared originally as important and integral parts of the authorʼs writings on a vast range of topics from linguistics and philology to history, geography, medicine, science, art, religion, spirituality, philosophy, etc. Such books included Varńa Vijiṋána, Varńa Vicitrá (eight parts) and Shabda Cayaniká (twenty-six parts). Like most great authors, Shrii Prabhat Ranjan Sarkar is a consummate storyteller, thus he used in those books a seemingly inexhaustible supply of anecdotes, personal experiences and interesting as well as educative references, in order to capture the readerʼs interest. And it is mostly those stories that have been excerpted to constitute the present book. Thus it is natural that in the stories contained in the present book, we will find, either at the beginnings of those stories or as footnotes, relevant references to the linguistic and other subjects of the original books. In this way the stories retain the authenticity of the original books.

points.body: In the present volume, Part 4 contains seventeen stories from Varńa Vicitrá Parts 7 and 8 which are translated from the original Bengali as the above-named books were not printed in English. Part 5 contains eight stories from Varńa Vicitrá Part 8 which are also translated in the present volume. The last two stories (ten stories in all) are from Shabda Cayaniká Part 1, which is available in English, but properly re-edited. Part 6 contains eight long stories from Shabda Cayaniká Part 1 and 2 also properly re-edited. At the end of this note the “Sources” for each story are included.

They take the reader on a journey into the little known world of “Dream and Reality”, evoking deep feelings of pathos. At the beginning of each such story the author sets the scene in a way that will help the reader to understand the inner spirit of the stories.

points.body: In this respect it will be useful to quote the following: “Actually, the dream state is a combination of subtle experiences collected from the mental world and vibrations collected from the waking state. Those vibrations which are gathered from the crude world oscillate constantly between truth and untruth, but those which come from the mental world are sometimes relative and sometimes non-relative truth. There is little opportunity for vibrational movement in the conviction of absence realized in deep sleep but we cannot reject this as non-existence. Anyhow, all this happens in the flow of consciousness, sometimes in a very natural, and sometimes in an unnatural rhythmic flow. This was consciousness or its negative, unconsciousness.”

points.body: The author used a particular shorthand for explaining the etymologies of words. Under this system, a minus sign (–) follows a prefix, and a plus sign (+) precedes a suffix. points.body: Every new translation is reviewed by a “first editor” who compares the English translation with the original Bengali or Hindi. Thereafter it is sent to the “second editors” to improve the standard of the English. On completion of the second editing, the final verification, which includes one more comparison with the original Bengali, is done by the Publication staff. Other important functions include the coordination of these different steps and the development and management of a global distribution and sales network.

points.body: The verbal root bat́ means to grow, to acquire strength, to exhibit strength. In common parlance, the ba that we get by adding d́a to the verbal root bat́ means “one that gathers strength or displays strength”. The banyan tree does not stop growing. So one meaning of ba (bat́ + d́a) is banyan tree. Bat́ > bad́a > baŕa.

points.body: In Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh, a banyan tree is colloquially referred to as bar. In Persian and Urdu it is called bargad. The banyan tree belongs to the family of trees which does not stop growing; it keeps on growing. There are many species ( 1 ) of banyan tree in the world; among them, the Chinese and Indian species are the most noteworthy. The Indian banyan tree (Banian indica) grows aerial roots ( 2 ) from its main trunk rather quickly. These aerial roots later grow into trunks. Some banyan trees have a large number of trunks. Sometimes it happens that even after the original trunk has been eaten up by white ants ( 3 ) [termites] or caterpillars, the tree survives and remains in good health due to its well-developed aerial roots. The banyan tree in the botanical garden of Kolkata and the banyan tree standing in the vicinity of Bagchi-Jamshedpur in Nadia District are estimated to be more than four thousand years old. In fact, the second one may be even older. Many people say that the banyan tree obtained its unending longevity as a boon from Sita. Let me briefly tell you that [mythological] story.

This river was formed from the union of rivers Nairanjana and Mohaniya, both originating from the south. At the time of the obsequies of Dasarath [father of Rama and Laksmana], Rama, Laksmana and Sita were staying on the bank of the Phalgu. However, the obsequies were delayed.

points.body: The son of King Balii was King Báńa. King Báńa was a devotee of Lord Shiva. Báńeshvar, one of the names of Lord Shiva, is derived from the name of King Báńa. The historical King Báńa was possibly a king of some part of Bengal. There are certain places in Bengal which are named after him; for example, Báńaeshvar and Báńagaŕ. In common parlance, one of the meanings of the word ba that we get by adding the suffix d́a to the verbal root bal is Balii, the demon King. It is this King Balii who is better known as MahaBalii. King Balii, who is still highly regarded in the most remote parts of Kerala in South India, is invariably associated with the name of Viśńu or Náráyańa. Náráyańa defeated King Balii not by physical strength but by the strength of intellect. The word ba that we get by adding the suffix d́a to the verbal root bal means that intellectual strength is the greatest strength, and it refers to Viśńu. ( 2 )

points.body: The word ba does not only mean one who is physically strong; it is equally applicable to one who is mentally or spiritually strong. That is why the word ba, which is used to mean the application of physical force, is also used to mean the application of mental or spiritual force. So, one of the meanings of ba, which we get by adding the suffix d́a to the verbal root bal is to create pressure, to create circumstantial pressure or to proceed according to a plan in order to attain some particular goal. Some people think that the word ba means to vilify someone. This is partly true. One can use the word ba when someone is vilified in order to pressurise that person into doing something. So the verbal root ba + d́a = ba means “to pressurise in order to attain a particular goal”.

points.body: Pat́olprasanna was a simple man who minded his own business, but his pious wife Smt. Begunbálá – well, who could withstand her speech! The torrential flow of words from her mouth was stronger than that of a western gale. Every day, she would religiously quarrel with Pat́olprasanna every fifteen minutes by the clock. She said that in this world, a man should work and one who did not work was sure to be ruined. The best kind of work was quarrelling. The kind of majesty that a serious quarrel invoked has hardly any comparison in the cosmos. When the quarrel reached its climax, Begunbálá would bring out her jewellery box, remove the ornaments from her body and put them in the box. Then she would put a lock on the box and check at least thrice to see that the box had been properly locked. After that, she would tie the key into a knot at the end of her saree and tuck it in her vest. Finally, she would hold the box in her hand and say, “Well, Mister, I am going now. I have decided to drown myself. Let me see which female ghost serves you food!”

Begunbálá with her jewellery box would not go to that pond to drown herself. She would go through the back door to another pond, which was generally used for cleaning kitchen utensils. Even its deepest part was so shallow that a small pot could not sink in it. Begunbálá would move one step forward and say, “Mister, I am dying … Mister, I am sinking!” After that, she would stand still in a pose and warn her husband again, “Let me see who serves you food!” Then she would move another step further. points.body: One of the meanings of the word bha that we obtain by adding the suffix d́a to the verbal root bha is “shining opulence”. There may be opulence of prestige, honour, money, quality or wisdom, but when that opulence is associated with welfare, then the word bha is used to indicate this. points.body: Yes, we were talking about the notorious Cáoyá-Cát́á [the amusing name means “always asking for”] Cát́ujje. He was an eminent person in Chinsura-Carakdaunga. I hope some of you know my acquaintance, Hyáḿlá Hoṋdal Hotá. Some of you must know him. (A farmer by profession, he hailed from Halimpur, Hooghly District, Khatian [ledger] No. 3 Plot No. 300). Hyáḿlá Hoṋdal [Hyáḿlá means “greedy”] was not a bad boy, but he was particularly fond of attending feasts. Quite often, he used to wangle an invitation to a feast by asking for it. Sometimes, he would eat at a feast given on the occasions of various rituals, such as shráddha [obsequies] and paite [the ceremony of putting on the holy thread sacramentally for the first time] without an invitation. He had long hair. While eating, he would bend his head in such a way that his face was screened by his hair. The host, when checking the guests to see who were invited and who were not, could not confirm whether he had actually been invited because his face could not be seen. His younger brother, Barśá Bádal, was not so resourceful. As a result, he was not lucky enough to get invitations to feasts.

points.body: He said, “I asked Cáoyá-Cát́á, 'Am I really invited today?ʼ Cáoyá-Cát́á at once replied, 'Certainly, of course. Not once, but hundred times, yes.ʼ After a brief pause, Cáoyá-Cát́á told me, 'Man has progressed a lot in observing formalities. Whatever it is, whether one sincerely likes formality or not, it is written on the wedding invitation card, ‘Blessing in place of formality is desirable’. But actually, everybody wants formality instead of blessing. You will notice that there is a practice of keeping a written record of who has presented what to the bride and the bridegroom in wedding homes. Obviously, such an account is maintained because there is a hankering, in the deepest recesses of the mind for these presents. Not only that, you will see that if somebodyʼs marriage takes place towards the end of the month, the ceremony of bau-bhát [the ceremony of a bride serving food for the first time to her husbandʼs kinsfolk] is not held then because by the end of the month, everybodyʼs pocket is empty. The guests may not come at all because they are unable to give presents. And those who do come would not be able to give costly presents. Keeping this in view, bau-bhát is arranged at the beginning of the next month a few days after the marriage. At that time, the guests are quite solvent. Moreover, not much money is spent on feeding because it is written on the invitation card that the entertainment of the guests will be in keeping with the rules of ‘guest control’. It means that just by giving a light refreshment, it is possible to squeeze an expensive gift.

But you are an intelligent, educated boy; you canʼt go to the invitation empty-handed. You must bring a few packets of canácur and d́álmut́ [snacks] in your pocket. In my house, there are good stainless steel plates and tumblers. I would naturally expect that you will put the canácur on the plate and eat it with satisfaction. In case there is load shedding [power cut] at that time, I shall entertain you, my guest, by fanning you with a hand fan. The well in my courtyard has the best water in Chinsura. It is not salty like the water of the Ganges. Whatever you eat will be immediately digested. Even if you bring four or five packets, you will see that by the time you reach home, they will all be digested.ʼ”

points.body: In the consonantal scheme of alphabets, the first letter in the ka group is ka and the last letter in the pa group is ma. Now the question is: why does ka come first and ma last? This world revolves around the process of creation, preservation and destruction. The seed of creation is a; that is why a comes first in the vowels. First creation, and only then do the rest follow. After that is u, the seed of preservation. So creation is spread over these three sounds. The combination of these three sounds is called ońḿ (a + u + m = ońḿ).

summary: Ka is the seed of action of Brahma. In other words, one part of the Supreme Brahma continues to exist as the cause while the other part is manifested in action.
points.body: Ka is the seed of action of Brahma. In other words, one part of the Supreme Brahma continues to exist as the cause while the other part is manifested in action. One part is the cause and the other part is the effect or objectivated cause. That is why this ka is called saḿvrttibodhicitta in Buddhist philosophy. Since ka is the seed of action, ka is therefore the first consonant; and since ma is the seed of destruction, ma is the last consonant.

points.body: I was talking about ouṋḿkára – a + u + m = ońḿ. But this om is meant for the manifested world. If one wants to use the seed of some positive sound for both the manifested and the unmanifested, then om will not do; one has to write oṋḿ [like Bengali symbol]. In this case, the candrabindu [the diacritical mark of a point in the crescent moon indicating a nasalised sound] connotes Nirguńa Brahma [Brahma without attributes]. This Brahma without attributes cannot be verbalised in utterance. So, in orthography, one first uses a point (a point has a position but no magnitude) and the longish sign that looks like a crescent moon under the point indicates the transformation from the negative to the positive aspect of attributes. In Sanskrit, it is called náda, that is, nirguńa saḿsthiti [the state of non-attributes] is transformed into Saguńa Brahma [the state of attributes] with the help of náda or sound. Please remember that it is not exactly a candrabindu [a point with a curve suggestive of the crescent moon]. It is something like the Bengali iishvara sign (a symbol put before the name of a deceased person). According to old custom, this nádabinducihna is used before the name of a dead person. When reading this nádabindu, we read it as iishvara. When a man is alive, the word shrii is used before his name; for example, Shrii Kumud Chandra Maiti. But the prefix Shrii cannot be used before his name after his death. The name Kumud Chandra Maiti will be written just after nadabindu and the name will be read as iishvara Kumud Chandra Maiti.

points.body: Another name of oṋḿkára is prańava, the etymological meaning of which is “that which propels towards the destination.” You are probably aware of the fact that in ancient times, in that age of superstition, not everyone had the right to articulate the word oṋḿkára. The outcastes and women were not only disallowed from uttering the word oṋḿ, even their right to hear the word was constrained. Hearsay has it that if any of them heard the oṋḿkára sound, molten lead would be poured into their ears to make them completely deaf. Verily, what an age of superstition it was! Such superstitions pervaded all walks of life. It was not only women who were tortured on account of this; men suffered no less. A story of social superstition comes to mind. The story is about one Subuddhi Roy of the Pathan dynasty.

On one particular occasion, some water from a Muslimʼs badná [a small pitcher with a slender spout] accidentally touched his face. The Brahman pundits convened a meeting. They unanimously resolved that it was a serious sin, a serious crime. Subuddhi Roy would have to perform a ceremonial expiation. Oh, I forgot to tell you that Subuddhi Roy at that time was the head of the Brahman community, a representative of the Brahmans.

points.body: As the Brahman community rose in arms against Subuddhi Roy, he became frightened to the extreme. He was made to seek the counsel of the pundits of Nabadwip [Navadviip] for the necessary mode of expiation. The pundits of Nabadwip gave the verdict that he had to perform tuśáńal práyashcitta [expiation with fire made from husks or chaff]. In tuśáńal práyashcitta, the guilty person had to stand before the fire when it was fully ablaze. The husks would be spread over an area covering sixty-four times the height of the person. The sinner or guilty person had to walk barefoot on it. If the sinner survived the ordeal, the expiation would be accomplished. And if the sinner died, the matter ended there.

points.body: One meaning of the Sanskrit verbal root mada is “what gives pleasure in sucking”. Etymologically, it means water, cordial, sharbat [sweet drink], hyacinth, fruit juice and any kind of fluid which comes under the category of drinks. The kind of thirst that one feels after consuming the items mentioned above is called mada + d́a = ma. For example, one feels thirsty when one takes chátu [flour made of barley, pigeon-pea, maize, etc.] in a small quantity of water. Again, one feels thirsty when taking poláo [a highly spiced dish of rice and meat boiled in clarified butter]. This kind of thirst for water is called jaltán.

points.body: Food (in the sense of the verbal root ma) which does not cause any trouble upon its ingestion is called ma. This kind of food does not require much chewing and usually goes down the throat almost as soon as it has been put into the mouth; for example, birikaláyer dál [blackgram pulse], kuler ambal, pát́ or pát-shák [green leaves of jute plant] with a touch of salt and pepper and items prepared with basella are quite wholesome and can easily be eaten. That is why, by adding the suffix d́a to the verbal root mada or by adding the suffix ka to the verbal root má, we get the word ma to mean this kind of food.

points.body: There lived a Brahman and his wife. The Brahman was a very good man, as simple and ever cheerful as Lord Shiva. His wife was also a very good person, but she was rather fond of eating – in particular, the attraction of basella was irresistible to her. Ut́hone yedike cái keval puiṋ dekhite pái [in whichever direction of the courtyard I look, only basella comes to view]. The Brahman also ate basella but did not like it much. After eating some pántá bhát [stale rice] and hot beguni [a fried snack prepared by dipping slices of brinjal in a thin paste of pulse powder] with a sprinkle of salt and pepper, he would leave the house for various kinds of work. His wife took care of the household chores. After some time, it was noticed that the Brahman was getting more and more emaciated while his wife was getting heavier by the day. The people of the locality enquired, “Oh Brahman, what has happened to you? You are getting thinner and thinner and your wife is becoming heavier and heavier! What is the mystery? Certainly, after treating you with a pot of stale rice and packing you off, your wife must be preparing seven hundred kinds of delicious food and eating them with relish afterwards.”

points.body: But people continued to say the same thing again and again. One day, the Brahman thought, “Since these people are so insistent, let me verify it.” That day, the Brahman, after going out through the main door, stealthily re-entered the house through the back door, tiptoed into the kitchen and lay down in the attic. He could not breathe heavily lest his wife, on hearing the sound of breathing, suspected that there was someone else present in the room. Most of the time, the Brahman had to put a silencer on his mouth to suppress the sounds of sneezing and coughing.

points.body: The Brahman kept watching and watching and watching. His wife, meanwhile, collected a huge pile – about one maund [82 lbs] of basella, basella leaves and basella paste and prepared a dry dish of basella. She then poured a liberal quantity of oil and fried basella stems and the bones of bhet́kii fish [a large, flat fish found in rivers] into it, dipped some green basella leaves in the basella paste and fried them like phuluri, made a paste of raw poppy seeds with salt and pepper, mixed it with boiled basella and made basella posta [basella-poppy seed preparation]. After that, she prepared shukto [bitter broth], postor baŕá [fried poppy seeds], jhiuṋe posta, chánár dálná [fresh cheese curry], jhál, jhol, ghant́a, caccaŕi, chyáṋcŕá, diḿler chakká, kuler ambal, birirdál [different delicious preparations], different kinds of pies and, finally, ciṋŕer páyes [a sweet prepared with milk and beaten rice] with nalenguŕ [date palm raw sugar].

After that, she entered the kitchen, arranged seven hundred pots and collected a huge quantity of rice piled so high that a cat would not be able to jump over it. Thus, she was engaged in completing the second part of the ritual. So many things! How can they be eaten with one hand! So the wife of the Brahman started using both hands.

points.body: It took quite a few hours before she finished her meal, leaving a huge pile of chewed-up food. The woman said to herself, “Truly, can this be called eating? Today, what I have put into my mouth is just chicken feed.” Then, a dark thought came to her mind. She thought, “I have taken so much pains to cook, more pains to eat and now, look, I should somehow make my way to the pond to quickly wash my mouth and then lie down to chew the betel leaves while someone else cleans the leftovers. points.body: The woman died. When he saw that his wife was dead, the Brahman started wailing. While crying loudly, he kept saying, “Please come here, whoever hears me, come and see at least once. Alas, what have I done! I did not want to kill my wife. I just wanted to frighten her, to discipline her. I never would have thought that she would die and cause me to be overwhelmed with sorrow. Please come, whoever hears me. Please come and see what has happened.”

points.body: The woman pressed as many sájápán as she could into a container and put the container in her vanity bag. Then, carrying the vanity bag in one hand and the huge bag on the other, she came out chewing a betel leaf and took her seat in the chariot. The Brahman often suffered from stomach trouble, so he came out sucking some jauṋgii hartuki ( 1 ) [black myrobalan] and wearing a waistbelt. He also put a belt loosely around the waist of his wife because a few days ago, she had had her stomach stitched. The woman mused, “Who knows how long it will take to reach heaven! Anyway, I have taken all the necessary items. Once I reach heaven, I shall start cooking the fine maluk rice and simultaneously prepare alur dam [a variety of highly seasoned thick curry made of potato]. For this reason, I have brought some potatoes from Nainital. I have also brought a tin of dhákái-ciṋŕe [Dhaka variety of beaten rice] as well as nalenguŕ [raw sugar prepared from new date juice] from Jessore. I shall prepare ciṋŕer páyes [porridge of beaten rice]. I have heard that gods take milk. But who knows whether that is cowʼs milk! They are probably supplied with some adulterated milk from a dairy from earth. And why should I bother so much! I have already brought a tin of powdered milk.”

points.body: After that, she took out a pán and, while giving it to the Brahman, said, “Look Brahman, you lack grace in everything. Everything of yours is ugly. You should have worn a fine dhoti and a finely frilled (gile kará) páiṋjábi [a loose-fitting upper garment, usually without a collar] made of very fine quality cotton (áddi). Instead, you are just wearing a short, eight-hand long dhoti and a phatuá [a loose, cotton waistcoat]. When people see them, they will only blame me. On such a day of joy, you are just sucking hartuki. Come, take two pieces of cháṋci pán [pure betel leaf]!”

points.body: In ancient times, people used the wood of the sal tree (indrakáśt́ha), marmelos tree (bel kát́h) and fig tree (ud́umbar) as firewood in religious sacrifices. There are several species of ud́umbar or d́umur [fig] of which the common fig and sacrificial fig [Ficus religiosa] are important. It is this sacrificial fig which is called ud́umbar or yájiṋad́umbar. Both these kinds of figs are good for the liver and kidney. They are also medicines for blood pressure. Sacrificial fig is more nutritious and more easily digestible than the common fig.

points.body: One meaning of the word ya is sacrificial fig. By and large, the fig is an exception in the world of fruits and flowers. When other flowers bloom or blossom, their inner parts are pushed outside. The fig ( 1 ) is also a flower, but when it blooms it turns inward.

points.body: That is why we think that the fig is a fruit; actually, it is a flower. Since it blossoms inside, we call it a fruit, and because we cannot see it bloom, we think that a fig flower is a rare thing which cannot be seen. When someone makes an appearance after a long time, we usually say to that person, “Whatʼs the matter? We donʼt see you at all these days! We wonder if you have turned into a fig flower!” A fig is called d́umar in the Angika language while in most parts of North India it is called gullar.

points.body: You must have heard of Phulawariishariif ( 2 ) in Magadha. In those days, Magadha was one of the great centres of Buddhist culture. The whole world looked up to Magadha for wisdom and spiritual wealth (upasampadá). There were many famous Buddhist monasteries in the land of Magadha. In the beginning, these were called Brahmavihár. Later, they came to be known as Baoddhavihár or Buddhist monasteries. Phullarháriibihár was one of the monasteries in Magadha. Phullarháriibihár was later renamed Phulawariishariif. In those days, milk and curd of excellent quality were available in Phullarháriibihár. Cowherds and curd sellers were also to be found in abundance. They were truly skilled in their craft.

summary: Once upon a time, a curd seller was travelling from Phulawariishariif to Ajimabad. On his way, he saw a vast expanse of sandy land along the nearby Ganges River
points.body: Once upon a time, a curd seller was travelling from Phulawariishariif to Ajimabad. On his way, he saw a vast expanse of sandy land along the nearby Ganges River. When he reached there, the tired curd seller sat under a tree to rest. He sat under the tree for quite some time. While resting, he became drowsy. By the way, I forgot to tell you that he did not have weighing instruments – on one side of the pole that he was carrying on his shoulders was a mund of curd and on the other side was a stone with a weight (ojan ( 3 )) of one mund.

points.body: The curd seller had thought that on reaching Ajimabad, he would get the stone broken into pieces of different weights – one seer, half seer, one-fourth seer, etc. But when he woke up, the curd seller was greatly surprised to find that his one mund stone had been broken into four pieces, from his curd emanated the fragrance of sandalwood, and the thin film that was on the curd had become four times thicker. At first, even after he reached Ajimabad ( 4 ), he did not realise the significance of the four pieces.

points.body: So he started selling the curd, using a spoon as an approximate measure. And, lo and behold, a strange thing happened! It was like the magic box [the earthen container] of Bhanumatii [a famous lady magician from ancient times]. The more curd he sold, the more it grew in quantity, and the film on top became thicker and thicker and thicker! People who came to buy only one seer at once wanted to buy one mund. And those who came to buy one mund wanted to buy ten munds! In one hour, he had sold curd to one lakh [one hundred thousand] inhabitants of Azimabad. The curd seemed to be inexhaustible. Just then, a famous astrologer passed by. When the curd seller saw him, he said,

points.body: “Sir, Panditjii [wise man], I have run into a strange problem. See what is happening. The more curd I sell, instead of becoming less, the original quantity becomes more! What strange magic is this! Not only that – while I was sleeping under a tree, my one mund stone spontaneously broke into four pieces.”

points.body: The astrologer was stunned. He at once cast the horoscope on a slate and started examining which planets were in, what the stars were, the ráshi [one of the twelve signs of the zodiac] and the lagna [the rising time of any zodiacal sign or the sign of the sunʼs transition to a zodiacal sign] of the tree under which the curd seller had sat, and at which particular point of time of the star and the day of the moon he had got up. After making all these calculations on the interactions of various planets and stars and other factors, he told the curd seller, “Look, you are passing through an excellent time now. Jupiter is auspicious and Saturn is extremely pleased. You should have become a king by now. But by mistake God has written ma in place of ra. As a result, although you have not become a king, you are enjoying good fortune. If you pay the astrologer liberally when giving his fee, he will make this good fortune continue for the rest of your life. In fact, whether you pay more or less, that is up to you. I am not going to ask you nor am I going to say ‘No’ if you pay.”

And another fig flower fell on your mund stone, hence the stone broke into four pieces. With the help of those stones as weights, you can sell as many seers of curd as you like at a time. There is no need to sell by approximate weight – you were suffering losses.”

It will be very beneficial for you. Itʼs not very costly, just about a lakh. You have already made a profit of three lakhs by selling curd. You have given me one lakh as my fees and one lakh for the talisman. And you are still left with one lakh. I shall not take the money even if you want to give it to me. points.body: With the pursuit of knowledge and subsequent acquisition of scholarship, human beings learn to exercise control over the mind. They train birds and animals to do various things. A restrained mind is the essence of all kinds of knowledge and learning. Otherwise, one can never learn anything nor can one acquire any knowledge and, even if one acquires knowledge, one cannot retain it. The word ya (by adding the suffix d́a to the verbal root yaj) is used for the type of effort by which a human acquires knowledge. It should be borne in mind that, generally, the word ya cannot be used for learning. Only the learning which one tries to acquire for oneʼs own development is called ya. Speaking about development through learning, I am reminded of a story.

points.body: You must have heard about a place called Singur. In very ancient times, Siḿhapur or Siuṋgur was the capital of Ráŕh. Although Singur was not as old as Bardhaman [Burdwan], it was older than most places in Bengal and India. Later, Singur was completely destroyed by the disastrous flooding of the Damodar River. Anyway, there were two rivers – Pulakitá and Ghrtáci – flowing by Siḿhapur. These rivers were the connecting links between Bhagiirathii and Damodar. Close to Siḿhapur, which was situated on the banks of the confluence of these two rivers, was a now-forgotten port called Siḿhalapát́an. It is said that from the port of Siḿhalpát́an, Vijay Singha, the prince of Ráŕh, set off for Siḿhal [Ceylon], and on reaching Siḿhal conquered the country. This is possibly the reason why the port was named Siḿhalpát́an.

points.body: In the course of time, the history of the ancient land of Ráŕh was forgotten, and the people of Ráŕh have also forgotten Siḿhalpát́an. Most of the water belonging to what we now call Hooghly District used to be drained near this port of Siḿhalpát́an. Siḿhapur or Singur, the capital, was situated near Siḿhalpát́an. At one time, Siḿhapur was not only the seat of royal power but also a centre of learning. In Siḿhapur and the surrounding vicinity there lived many great scholars. Today, that Singur is extinct.

points.body: I am talking about the Singur of the medieval period. Singur suffered the same fate as that of other ancient cities. During that time, a pundit started a private school in Singur. From the viewpoint of this 20 century, it is not possible to say anything definite about his scholarship or lack of it, but it is said that in some of the houses in Hooghly District, a tape recording of the punditʼs conversation with a washerwoman can still be found.

points.body: You must have heard of the place called Nasipur. Nasipur existed even during the period of the Pathans. During that age, there lived a rajakinii [washerwoman)] who possessed crores of rupees. She would lie down on gold coins. But she would never spend any money, not even a cowry, let alone a copper coin. She said that to spend one cowry meant to lose one rib. For a long time, the washerwoman had been cooking rice in a leaking pot and had been using a broken hand fan to fan herself. This was how she was happily spending her days. But fate was against her. One day, after washing some rice grains and while pouring them into the pitcher, the pitcher cracked from top to bottom from the impact of the rice. The washerwoman felt sad – not because of the cracked pitcher but because so many rice grains that had spilled on the stove were wasted. More saddening was the fact that the fire on the stove was extinguished by the rice and some rice water had spilled on it. With a very heavy heart, she went to Singur. When she reached there, after much bargaining she purchased a pitcher, a hand fan and a small pot of curd because her granddaughter had been pestering her for curd for quite some time.

summary: She told the curd seller, “Please give me the residual watery dregs of curd lying in your large pot and donʼt ask any money for it, please.” Thereafter, the was
points.body: She told the curd seller, “Please give me the residual watery dregs of curd lying in your large pot and donʼt ask any money for it, please.” Thereafter, the washerwoman started walking towards Nasipur with her donkey. On the way, she came across the private school of the pundit we had mentioned earlier. She heard with her own ears the pundit saying, “I have turned so many donkeys into horses, so many horses into humans. Some of them are teaching in colleges, some are writing voluminous books, and I have failed to change you into a horse. Where shall I hide this sorrow?” Then he asked the pupil to kneel down, putting a few pieces of burnt earth under the pupilʼs knees and placing two bricks on his hands. After that, he said, “Remain like that with your tongue out; only then will you learn your lesson.”

points.body: The washerwoman could not hold her excitement any longer. She told the Pundit, “Sir, I have five hundred donkeys. For the time being, you take this one at least. First turn it into a horse and then turn it into a human. By selling a horse I can earn more than what I can by selling a donkey and by selling a human ( 1 ), I shall get much more money.”

points.body: The students said, “Oh, no. He is a one hundred percent pure Englishman. He was on his way to this country on a plane, when suddenly he fell out of the window like a ripe mango. And look where he fell! Into the fathomless waters of the Black Sea. For one hour, he swam in different styles: sometimes going underwater and sometimes using back strokes. After one hour, he reached the shore uninjured except that his complexion had turned black. If one remains in the water of the Black Sea for such a long time, can one avoid turning black? Since his arrival here, he has been washing his face with soap three hundred times every day and using many other cosmetics to regain his original complexion. Once it so happened that because of intense rubbing, the skin on his face peeled off. Since then, he has stopped trying to regain his original complexion. He said, 'Since I now live in the country of black people, it is better to look black. A black human is also a human. In fact, the brilliance of learning makes the black complexion more glittering.”

points.body: When we burn an object, the exterior is destroyed by fire, but the interior becomes soft with the heat of the fire. When we ignite an object, both the interior and exterior are destroyed by contact with the fire and are turned into ashes. We burn a brinjal. We ignite the wick of a lamp. When the exterior of an object becomes more or less burnt while the interior does not become very soft but is only slightly affected, we call it singeing. For singeing (jhalsáno), the word ra is applied by adding the suffix d́a to the verbal root rá.

points.body: In the old days, plays were often very melodramatic. The dialogue of a drama should be natural but it is slightly different from the normal conversations of mundane everyday life. In daily life, when we talk among ourselves, we do not want anyone else to hear us, nor do we think of compelling others to hear us. We confine the conversation to ourselves. But in a dramatic dialogue, the actors have to bear in mind that the audience or spectators should be able to hear what they are saying and should understand from their gestures themselves what they want to say. This is the main difference between normal conversations and dramatic dialogues. Of course, there are other differences as well.

points.body: In those days, most dramas were melodramas. Once, a famous opera troupe came from Kolkata to our village. I went to watch the performance along with my grandmother (the expression in those days was “to go and listen to operatic songs”). The king was in a dialogue with his queen. The king, with his tin foil robe, tin foil crown and tin foil-wrapped weapon, was getting ready to go to the battlefield with much fanfare. At that moment, the king and queen were conversing in a melodramatic fashion. The queen was saying, “Paráńeshvar, práńanátha! Kotha yáo pheliyá ámáre?” [“Oh, heart of my life, Oh, Lord of my life, where are you going, leaving me behind?”]

points.body: The verbal root ruś means not bursting out in anger, to suppress anger. Bursting out in anger is called krodha. But when anger is suppressed, we call it roś. Krodha can be understood immediately, but it takes time to understand roś. Suppose somebody was angry with you and subsequently everything became normal and you have probably forgotten about the incident. Suppose, after quite some time, you invite that person to dinner and he replies harshly, “Iʼm not eating today.” You then realise that he has suppressed anger in his mind. This is called roś.

points.body: Do you know Káliikrpá Bhat́cáj [Kalikripa Bhattacharya] of Shantipur? But how could you know? It happened such a long time ago. It was during the British period. Kálii Bhat́cáj was employed in the civil service in Kashii [Benaras], drawing a fat salary. In those days, anybody who had some knowledge of English could easily get a job. It is said that in those days, the life of a particular class of people consisted of four forms. The first form was for admission to an English medium school. The second form was to obtain a certificate from the school after learning elementary English. The third form was the application form to join the railway service. The fourth form was the platform where one would stand with a railway flag in hand. Kálii Bhat́cháj was much better than these people. Previously, when he was the station master of Railways, he spoke English fluently.

Kálii Bhat́cáj did not feel in the least scared. But in order to evoke their pity and to apprise them of his poverty, he said, “I, poor man sir, even then forty leaves [forty plates made of leaves] fall daily in my house sir. See my condition, sir. I am a poor man, sir. Even then I have to feed forty people daily. Please understand my situation, sir.”
